extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in natural science, field geologists, and school teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and observable features used to detect past continental glaciation, infer ice-sheet extent and movement, and interpret associated sea-level/land-elevation changes in North America during the ice age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glaciated appearance of ledges, striæ, and transported bowlders
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual glaciated appearance of the ledges, striæ, and transported bowlders is taken as proof of the presence of an ice-sheet (example given for Mount Washington).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: two transported boulders nearly 100 pounds identical with ledges several miles distant; surface rocks riven by frost and covered by lichens obscuring embossment and striation. These combined observations (striations + erratics + matching lithology) are presented as decisive evidence that an ice-sheet passed over high summits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of glacier movement direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Direction of ice movement inferred from glacial markings (striations), orientation/trend of moraines, and directions in which bowlders/erratics were transported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited observations: Packard's glacial markings in Hamilton Inlet indicating northeast run or southeast on southern coast; bowlders transported northeast and northwest in Arctic islands; trends of ground-moraine hummocks correspond to local ice-current directions (e.g., southeast near Newburyport to south 10° west in Connecticut Valley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distances of boulder/erratic transport used as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured distances that erratics and fossils have been transported are used to infer scope and vigor of ice movement and prevailing directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported distances: New England average 12–15 miles (rarely >100); Ohio many stones >100 miles; Iowa/Wisconsin native copper erratics 300–465 miles; fossils at Baton Rouge possibly from Canada West ~1,200 miles; auriferous quartz at Natchez possibly from Montana ~1,800 miles. Greatest distances associated with southwest-directed transport, possibly aided by topography and connected valleys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground-moraine (lower till) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground-moraine (lower till) is compact, sometimes clayey, full of small scratched far-traveled stones in a forced position, with iron coloring matter in the ferrous (protoxide) condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground-moraine is least noticed on active glaciers (inaccessible between ice and earth) but was likely the most abundant form in continental glaciers; it develops into lenticular hummocks in middle New England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper till and terminal moraine characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper till (the capping of hummocks and the material of terminal moraines) is loose, fragments are rough and not far removed from source, color often yellowish red from ferric oxide; terminal moraines are like upper till but often show oxidation throughout their whole mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal moraines are expected to be similar to upper till because fragments fronting the glacier consist of recently deposited material. Meltwater streams acting on moraines can produce sloping plains of gravel and sand or modify unstratified drift; the thickness and oxidation of terminal moraine mass distinguishes it from thin oxidized upper till.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lenticular hills as expression of ground-moraine
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground-moraine is developed into lenticular hills — oblong rounded hummocks sometimes up to 200 feet high — whose trend corresponds to the direction of the local ice-current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These hummocks are composed mostly of lower till with a capping of upper till; their orientation can be used to infer ice-flow directions in the neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapped morainic lines as determiners of ice-sheet limits and topography
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct lines (outer and inner series) of terminal moraines trace the outer margin(s) and internal limits of the glaciated area and determine regional topography (example: Long Island 'backbone').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outer moraine series traced from Nantucket across islands and through New Jersey into Pennsylvania and Ohio; inner moraine follows Cape Cod shore, Rhode Island south shore, and parts of Long Island. Topographic consequences include ridge elevations (e.g., Long Island highest point 384 ft) and asymmetric slopes (sandy southern slope vs clay cliffs north).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of kames and kame-lines with moraines
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines of kames (and related features) occupying watersheds or divides can be correlated with terminal moraines and used to map morainic systems across regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Newberry's line of kames along the watershed between Ohio and Lake Erie correlates with modified drift fringing the terminal moraine; similar kame-lines and loops occur across the Midwest and can indicate multiple morainic loops and confluent ice streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Looped and shore-following moraines indicate valley-guided glacier flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Moraines forming loops that follow lake shores (e.g., Lake Michigan, Green Bay, Keweenaw Bay, Lake Superior) suggest that glaciers followed individual valleys and continued to flow while material was available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These loop patterns and shore-conformable moraines show valley-guided flow paths and localized extensions of ice-streams. Absence of glacial deposits in lee of highlands (e.g., 'Lead-region of the Northwest') indicates flow shielding by topography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of erratic lithology to infer source regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of erratic rock types on moraines or ridges and matching them to distant ledges allows inference of transport direction and source provinces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Palisade traps in Brooklyn and New Haven red sandstones on Long Island matched to Connecticut/Hudson Valley ledges; matching lithology across distances supports northwest provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submarine contours and submerged pre-glacial river-channels as evidence of former elevations
rubrics_metrics.description: Submarine contour mapping that reveals continuations of river valleys out to sea (e.g., Connecticut and Hudson) and large fiords/linear lakes indicate prior lower sea levels or land elevation changes since the glacial period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: Connecticut formerly flowed around east end of Long Island; Hudson channel continues 70–80 miles out to sea. Absence of deltas at present mouths suggests comparatively recent submergence; similar submerged channels off Long Island and Cape Cod are cited as fiords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dredged Tertiary fossils on continental banks indicate submerged plains
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding Tertiary fossils on submarine banks (e.g., George's and Great Banks) identical to those of adjacent unsubmerged plains supports hypothesis that a low broad plain has been submerged since the glacial period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dredging these banks produced fossils similar to those in unsubmerged parts of the plain, offering a crucial test and evidence for a formerly subaerial plain now drowned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratigraphic / borehole evidence for former land elevation and lower sea level
rubrics_metrics.description: Excavation depths of Tertiary rocks overlain unconformably by orange sand coeval with glacial drift, and borehole sequences in lower Louisiana showing post-glacial deposits over orange sand over eroded Tertiaries, imply significant former incision and lower sea levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contour lines (e.g., 1,000-foot depth suggesting riverbed continuation into Gulf), and the need for Gulf waters to have been hundreds of feet lower are used to argue for at least several hundred feet of elevation change in the glacial period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical criteria for glacier motion (heat, shear, meltwater role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Molecular theories and physical observations: motion of glacier ice is proportional to heat present; shearing the ice requires many times its weight (Moseley: 30–40×); melted ice is very susceptible to gravity and meltwater flow produces greater motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agassiz's view emphasized heat/expansion by freezing and meltwater percolation making ice flow 'up-hill' toward the sun; such principles can explain how ice moves over elevations higher than its source without invoking massive uplift of land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and mapping of terminal moraines refute iceberg-only drift hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence and mapped lines of terminal moraines remove a major objection to explaining glaciation by icebergs alone (question: 'Where are the terminal moraines?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By showing continuous moraine lines across continental margins and inland, the glacial theory gains support against the iceberg-transport hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, hands-on pedagogy for teaching physiology
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach physiology with as much practical work as possible: provide a suitable text and a human skeleton, study bones/muscles/skin/circulatory/respiratory/digestive systems with plates and specimens, demonstrate a dissection (chloroform a cat) and then have pupils take turns dissecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class format: no strict recitations; pupils free to ask any classmate questions; dissection to 'clinch' facts rather than be exhaustive; follow Foster and Langley; supplement with birds, insects, fish, frogs, tadpoles; aim to develop observation and scientific method rather than produce expert dissectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum selection and sequencing for novice physiology classes
rubrics_metrics.description: For students aged ~16–21 and in under-resourced schools, focus on bones, muscles, skin, circulatory, respiratory and digestive systems and defer the nervous and reproductive systems as too abstruse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After covering core anatomical systems and practical dissections, review the text and proceed to comparative physiology and anatomy; adapt depth to time/material constraints and local prejudices against physiology teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical indicators of successful science teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Success measured by pupils' sustained interest (e.g., summer collecting of flora/fauna) and observable improvements in other subjects (quicker, clearer observation, more accurate reasoning, keener criticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher claims that pupils who took physiology performed better in Latin and mathematics; such transfer of observational and reasoning skills is cited as proof of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of exemplary scientific investigation (Pasteur model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good scientific investigation is characterized by strictness and severity of methods that make conclusions nearly unerring and give them the force of demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pasteur's work is praised for opening new research paths, offering clews for follow-up research, and exemplifying severe methods that yield predictive, demonstrable results; such methodological rigor is recommended as a model for investigators.
